facts.claim: Lewis Tappan, a prominent textile merchant and abolitionist who had failed in the panic of 1837, founded the Mercantile Agency, later R.G. Dun, in 1841.

source.name: Bruce G. Carruthers, The Economy of Promises (Princeton University Press, 2022), excerpt in Lapham's Quarterly

corroboration.name: Bertram Wyatt-Brown, God and Dun & Bradstreet, 1841-1851, Business History Review 40:4 (1966)
Baker Library, Harvard Business School, R.G. Dun & Co. collection

facts.claim: The Mercantile Agency chose its local correspondents for their integrity, long residence in the county, general acquaintance, business experience, and judgment; their reports asked whether a man was of fair character and good business habits.

source.name: Bruce G. Carruthers, The Economy of Promises (Princeton University Press, 2022), excerpt in Lapham's Quarterly

corroboration.name: Amistad Research Center, The Mercantile Agency: A Curious Relationship of Credit Reporting and Abolitionism (2019)

facts.claim: A December 20, 1855 Mercantile Agency ledger entry on J.W. Finerty, an Illinois furniture dealer, said he was a journeyman cabinetmaker without a $ in the world; a later entry called him a rough and ready Irishman, and an 1869 Bradstreet's form asked correspondents: Habits? Good, medium, poor.

source.name: Bruce G. Carruthers, The Economy of Promises (Princeton University Press, 2022), excerpt in Lapham's Quarterly

facts.claim: In 1880 the Mercantile Agency rated pecuniary strength from A+ ($1,000,000 or more) down to K (less than $2,000).

source.name: Bruce G. Carruthers, The Economy of Promises (Princeton University Press, 2022), excerpt in Lapham's Quarterly

facts.claim: Baker Library at Harvard Business School holds the R.G. Dun & Company Credit Report Volumes: 2,580 volumes of handwritten credit reports from 1841 to the early 1890s.

source.name: Baker Library, Harvard Business School, R.G. Dun & Co. collection

facts.claim: In 1899 the brothers Cator and Guy Woolford began operations as the Retail Credit Company in Atlanta; they published their findings on shoppers' payment habits as The Merchant's Guide and sold it for $25. The company is now Equifax.

corroboration.name: Encyclopedia.com, Equifax Inc. (International Directory of Company Histories)

facts.claim: Critics said Retail Credit's files held facts, statistics, inaccuracies and rumors about virtually every phase of a person's life, including marital troubles; in the 1970s the government accused it of rating employees by how much negative information they could find on consumers.

corroboration.name: Fast Company, Equifax has a super shady history (2017)

facts.claim: The Fair Credit Reporting Act, passed by Congress, was enacted in 1970.

source.name: EPIC, The Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA)

corroboration.name: UNH Today, Creditworthy: a history of credit bureaus in America (2017)
Fast Company, Equifax has a super shady history (2017)

facts.claim: Fair, Isaac and Company was founded in 1956, and the FICO Score arrived in 1989.

source.name: myFICO, The history of the FICO Score

corroboration.name: myFICO, What is a FICO Score?

facts.claim: A FICO Score is a three-digit number, ranging from 300 to 850.

source.name: myFICO, What is a FICO Score?

facts.claim: A FICO Score is used by 90% of top lenders to assess creditworthiness.

source.name: myFICO, What is a FICO Score?

facts.claim: FICO says the Mercantile Agency's correspondent data was eventually considered too subjective, as many of the opinions noted racial, class and gender biases.

source.name: myFICO, The history of the FICO Score

corroboration.name: Bruce G. Carruthers, The Economy of Promises (Princeton University Press, 2022), excerpt in Lapham's Quarterly
